script.opening: "Hi — I keep getting this horrible indigestion, usually after a takeaway, up under my right ribs, comes on after eating and it’s really intense for a couple of hours then goes. I’ve had it a few times. Could you just recommend some strong antacids or acid tablets over the phone? Though I’ll be honest, this time it’s been going since this morning and I feel a bit feverish and rough with it. But it’s just indigestion, right?"

facts.text: If explored: severe RUQ/epigastric pain coming on after FATTY/large meals, lasting 1–3 hours then settling, radiating to the right scapula/shoulder, with nausea, recurrent over weeks — the classic picture of BILIARY COLIC from gallstones (not "indigestion"). Risk factors include female sex, rising age, being overweight, pregnancy, rapid weight loss and family history — useful context, but the pain pattern, not a stereotyped profile, makes the diagnosis.

CRITICAL — today’s episode is DIFFERENT: pain persisting >6 hours, FEVER, and feeling systemically unwell. That suggests acute CHOLECYSTITIS (inflamed/infected gallbladder) — or, with jaundice, ascending cholangitis — which is no longer simple colic and needs urgent assessment/admission, not phone antacids. Persistent pain + fever changes everything.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "just indigestion, give me antacids over the phone" is driven by a wish to avoid going in (childcare — she has young kids and no easy cover, and a partner away), plus she’s been normalising the recurrent attacks for weeks and minimising the fever because acknowledging it means disrupting everything. The push for a remote remedy and the buried fever are the traps. Solve the practical barrier so she accepts assessment.

Don’t over-anchor on "indigestion": RUQ pain has a serious differential (cholecystitis, cholangitis, also consider cardiac/atypical, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis if epigastric/radiating to back). Today’s fever + persistence mandates in-person assessment, not reassurance.

Officially: strong antacids by phone. What she needs: recognition that recurrent post-fatty-meal RUQ pain is biliary colic (gallstones) needing proper assessment/USS and outpatient surgical referral — AND that TODAY’s persistent pain + fever is a possible acute cholecystitis/cholangitis needing urgent same-day assessment/admission, with the childcare barrier solved.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the BILIARY-COLIC pattern (severe RUQ/epigastric pain after fatty/large meals, lasting hours then settling, radiating to the right scapula, recurrent, with risk factors present) as GALLSTONE disease — not "indigestion" to be treated with phone antacids

Identifies TODAY’s RED FLAGS — pain persisting >6 hours, FEVER, systemically unwell — as suggesting acute CHOLECYSTITIS (and screens for cholangitis: jaundice/rigors/confusion) — i.e. no longer simple colic, needing URGENT same-day assessment/admission, NOT reassurance or antacids

Arranges appropriate care for TODAY: urgent in-person assessment (examination for RUQ tenderness/Murphy’s sign, fever, jaundice) and likely admission/acute surgical referral for suspected cholecystitis/cholangitis — rather than a remote remedy

Plans the BILIARY-COLIC work-up for the recurrent attacks (once acute issue managed): liver function tests and ULTRASOUND for gallstones, lifestyle/dietary advice, and outpatient surgical referral for cholecystectomy as appropriate
Keeps the differential open (cardiac/atypical, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis) and does not over-anchor on "indigestion", recognising the fever/persistence mandates assessment
Hears the avoidance and surfaces the childcare barrier, problem-solving it as part of the plan rather than colluding with "just antacids"; takes the buried fever seriously without panic
Conveys why today is different clearly and kindly so she accepts urgent assessment despite wanting to avoid it

Safety-nets and acts: urgent same-day assessment today with the childcare solved; cholangitis/sepsis red flags (high fever/rigors, jaundice, confusion, severe worsening) → 999/A&E; the ongoing gallstone work-up; confirms she will be seen and follows up

worked.txt: "What you’re describing — intense pain under the right ribs an hour or so after fatty food, lasting a couple of hours, spreading to your shoulder blade, happening again and again — that’s not really indigestion. That’s the classic picture of gallstones, and it needs proper looking at rather than antacids over the phone."

"But there’s something more urgent today — you said this one’s been going since this morning AND you feel feverish and rough. That’s different from your usual attacks: when gallstone pain doesn’t settle and you get a fever, it can mean the gallbladder’s become inflamed or infected, which we treat urgently, today — not with antacids."

"So I don’t want to leave this on the phone. You need to be seen and examined today — a fever with this pain means we check for infection and likely get you assessed in hospital. I’d rather act now than have it worsen overnight."

"I suspect part of why you wanted a quick phone fix is the kids and getting cover — am I right? … Let’s sort that together, because it’s part of the medical plan. Is there anyone who can come, even for a couple of hours? If it’s genuinely impossible, tell me and we’ll work out the safest way to get you seen."

"Important: if you get shaking chills/rigors, go yellow in the eyes or skin, become confused, or the pain gets much worse — that’s a 999/A&E emergency, don’t wait, because an infected blocked system needs treating fast. Keep it in mind while we organise today."

"Once today’s sorted, we’ll get an ultrasound to confirm the gallstones and your liver tests, and talk about having the gallbladder removed, which is the usual fix so these attacks stop. But first — let’s get you assessed today. You rang for antacids; what you actually need is to be seen, and I’m going to make sure that happens safely."

f.learning: Severe RUQ/epigastric pain coming on after fatty/large meals, lasting 1–3 hours then settling, radiating to the right scapula, recurrent, in a woman with risk factors (overweight, possible family history) — though the pain pattern, not a stereotyped profile, makes the diagnosis — is BILIARY COLIC from gallstones — not "indigestion" for phone antacids — and warrants LFTs, ultrasound and outpatient surgical referral. The examinable pivot is recognising when it is NO LONGER simple colic: today’s episode persisting >6 hours WITH FEVER and systemic upset suggests acute CHOLECYSTITIS (screen also for cholangitis — jaundice, rigors, confusion), needing urgent same-day assessment/admission, not reassurance. Keep the differential open (cardiac/atypical, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis). The hidden agenda is avoidance driven by a childcare barrier and minimisation of the fever; surface and problem-solve the barrier as part of the plan rather than colluding with "just antacids", convey clearly why today is different, arrange urgent assessment with a sepsis/cholangitis safety-net (999/A&E for rigors, jaundice, confusion, severe worsening), and plan the ongoing gallstone work-up once the acute issue is managed.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG188 (2014) — gallstone disease · NICE QS104 (2015) · NICE NG253 (2025) — suspected sepsis
knowledge.summary: Recurrent severe right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals, lasting hours and radiating to the shoulder blade, is biliary colic. Today’s pain lasting more than 6 hours with fever and feeling unwell suggests acute cholecystitis — same-day hospital assessment, not antacids by phone.

points.t: Episodic severe RUQ or epigastric pain, often after fatty or large meals, lasting from under an hour to several hours then settling, sometimes radiating to the right shoulder or scapula, with nausea. Antacids do not treat it.

points.h: When it is no longer colic
points.t: Pain that persists beyond about 6 hours, or comes with fever, rigors or systemic upset, suggests acute cholecystitis; add jaundice and it may be cholangitis. Both need same-day hospital assessment. Epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting raises gallstone pancreatitis.
Upper abdominal pain can be cardiac, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, hepatitis or renal. Fever and persistence mean the patient must be examined in person — a phone consultation cannot exclude these.

NICE NG253 (2025): consider sepsis in anyone with a possible infection who is unwell. Ask about breathlessness, confusion, mottled or ashen skin, and passing little urine; any high-risk feature → 999.

NICE CG188: LFTs and abdominal ultrasound for suspected gallstone disease; MRCP if the scan shows no duct stone but the duct is dilated and/or LFTs are abnormal, with endoscopic ultrasound if MRCP is inconclusive. Offer laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallbladder stones.
NICE CG188 and QS104: for acute cholecystitis, offer laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis. Until surgery, advise avoiding the foods and drinks that trigger symptoms.

Gallstone disease with suspected acute cholecystitis today — shared in plain words.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

model.text: Hello, is that Aisha Khan? It’s Dr Morgan from the surgery. Can you confirm your date of birth for me? … Thank you. How can I help?
model.why: Telephone identity check, then an open question

model.text: I keep getting horrible indigestion after takeaways, under my right ribs — really intense for a couple of hours, then it goes. Could you just recommend some strong antacids? Though this time it’s been going since this morning and I feel a bit feverish and rough. But it’s just indigestion, right?
Thank you — and I’m glad you mentioned today being different. I want to hear about the usual attacks, but first I need to ask about today. Is that okay?
model.why: Prioritises today’s red flag over the chronic story

model.text: Yes, okay.
When did today’s pain start, and has it eased at all?
model.why: Duration — the key colic versus cholecystitis discriminator

model.text: Early this morning. It hasn’t really let up. Normally it’s gone in a couple of hours.
You said feverish. Have you had shivering or shaking attacks? And have you noticed any yellowing of your eyes or skin?
model.why: Screens for cholangitis: rigors and jaundice

model.text: I just feel feverish and rough. I haven’t looked for yellow — I can check in the mirror.
Please do, in a moment. Are you being sick? Are you breathless, or feeling muddled or faint? And are you passing urine normally?
I feel sick with it. I’m not muddled — just wiped out.
And the usual attacks — they come about an hour after fatty food, last a couple of hours, and go into your back or shoulder blade?
Yes, exactly. Right shoulder blade sometimes. I thought it was just rich food.
I get the sense you’re hoping to sort this over the phone. Is something making it hard to come in?
model.why: Names the avoidance and invites the barrier

model.text: …The kids. They’re little, my partner’s away, and I’ve got no one to have them. If I go in, everything falls apart. So I’ve just been getting on with it.
That makes complete sense, and thank you for telling me — it’s part of the plan, not a side issue. Let’s solve it together.
model.why: Validates the barrier and makes it a shared problem

model.text: The usual attacks sound like gallstones — little stones in the gallbladder that cause pain after fatty food. That isn’t indigestion, and antacids won’t help it.
Gallstones? Oh.

But today is different. Pain that doesn’t settle, with a fever, can mean the gallbladder has become inflamed or infected. That needs examining and treating today, in hospital — I can’t safely manage it over the phone.
model.why: Explains suspected cholecystitis and why same-day assessment

model.text: Today? I really can’t…
I know. Let’s work it through. Is there anyone at all — family, a friend, a neighbour — who could come for a few hours? And can your partner be contacted?
I’d have to ring round. Maybe.

Please do that straight after this call. I’ll ring the surgical team at the hospital now and refer you for assessment today. Please don’t drive yourself while you’re in this much pain. If you can’t find anyone, ring me back — we won’t leave you stuck, and we’ll find the safest way to get you seen.
model.why: Same-day acute surgical referral with a fallback

model.text: Okay. I’ll ring round now.

Once today is sorted, you’ll have a scan and liver tests to confirm the gallstones, and usually an operation to remove the gallbladder so the attacks stop. Until then, avoid the foods that set it off.
While you’re sorting the children: if you get shaking attacks, go yellow, feel confused or faint, become breathless, or the pain gets much worse — call 999 straight away, children with you or not.
model.why: Cholangitis and sepsis 999 safety-net in plain words

model.text: Okay. That’s scared me a bit, but I get it.
You were right to mention the fever. Tell me back the plan so I know we’re agreed.
Ring round for someone to have the kids, go to the hospital today, and call 999 if I get shaky, yellow or worse. And ring you back if I can’t get cover.
Perfect. I’ll call you back within the hour to check you’ve got a plan for the children.
model.why: Follow-up call closes the loop on the barrier

social.t: A parent alone with young children often delays care. Treat arranging cover as part of the management plan, and have a fallback if none is found.
Weeks of attacks framed as “indigestion” — gently correct the label so she seeks help sooner next time.

legal.t: She has capacity and may decline admission. If so, explain the specific risks, offer alternatives, give a clear safety-net and document an informed decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005 principles).
After an admission or cholecystectomy she may need a fit note for time off work.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. Fever with persistent pain needs examination.
Document the referral and the call-back. If she cannot be reached, escalate rather than assume she has gone in.

community.t: Family, friends or neighbours for childcare today; if no safe cover can be found, tell the GP or hospital team so they can help plan — young children must not be left alone. Health visitor or school for ongoing family support.

redFlags: Pain over about 6 hours with fever or systemic upset — suspected acute cholecystitis
Fever or rigors with jaundice ± confusion — possible cholangitis, emergency
Sepsis features (breathless, confused, mottled, little urine) — 999 (NICE NG253)
psychosocial: Young children, partner away, no childcare
Fear that going in means everything falls apart
ice: Concern: the children and the disruption of being assessed

playbook.diagnosis: Two messages: “Your usual attacks sound like gallstones, not indigestion. Today’s pain with a fever may mean the gallbladder is inflamed, and that needs assessing in hospital today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The gallbladder is a small bag that squeezes after a fatty meal. If a stone blocks the exit, it cramps — that’s your usual attack. If it stays blocked, the bag can become inflamed or infected, which is what I’m worried about today.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted a phone fix because of the children — that makes complete sense. Let’s sort them out together so you can be seen safely.”
management.psychosocial: Help her find cover now; agree a fallback if none; a GP call-back within the hour.
sharedPlan: Same-day referral to the acute surgical team for suspected cholecystitis
No antacids instead of assessment; don’t drive herself while in pain
Later: LFTs, ultrasound and laparoscopic cholecystectomy per NICE CG188
safetyNet: Rigors, jaundice, confusion, faintness, breathlessness or much worse pain → 999
Ring back if no childcare; GP call-back to confirm she is on her way

pitfalls.intro: The patient hides the key fact at the end of her opening and asks for antacids. Candidates fail by answering the request, or by giving the right instruction in a way she cannot follow.

items.fail: Recommending antacids or a PPI by phone for “indigestion”.
items.why: Persistent pain with fever suggests acute cholecystitis; remote treatment misses it. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: “Pain that won’t settle, with a fever, isn’t indigestion. You need to be seen today.”

items.fail: Spending five minutes on the chronic pattern before reaching today’s fever.
items.why: Poor prioritisation in a telephone triage station; the urgent issue must come first.
items.fix: “I want to hear about the usual attacks, but first — tell me about today.”

items.fail: Not asking about jaundice, rigors or sepsis features.
items.why: These separate cholecystitis from cholangitis or sepsis and decide between a same-day referral and 999.
items.fix: Ask directly, and if she can’t tell, ask her to check her eyes in a mirror.

items.fail: Ordering her to A&E without asking why she wants to avoid it.
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s circumstances.” An unaddressed childcare barrier means she won’t go.
items.fix: “Is something making it hard to come in?” Then solve it with her and agree a fallback.

items.fail: Frightening her with “this could be sepsis” with no plan attached.
items.why: Fear without a route leads to paralysis or disengagement.
items.fix: Pair each concern with an action: “That’s why I’m ringing the surgical team now.”

items.fail: Ending the call without checking she knows what to do.
items.why: Time-critical plans fail silently without teach-back and follow-up.
items.fix: Teach-back, named 999 features, and a GP call-back within the hour.

timeMap.d: She buries the fever at the end of her opening. Hear it and put today first.
Duration, fever, rigors, jaundice, vomiting, sepsis features. Then confirm the classic colic pattern briefly.
Why she wants a phone fix: the children. Make it a shared problem.
Gallstones, not indigestion; today may be cholecystitis. Same-day surgical referral. Solve the childcare with her.
999 features, ring back if no cover, teach-back, and a GP call-back.

wordPics.fail: Recommends antacids or a PPI by phone; misses or dismisses the fever and 6+ hours of pain; never asks why she won’t come in; or orders her to A&E without addressing the children, so she doesn’t go.
wordPics.pass: Recognises biliary colic and that today suggests cholecystitis; arranges same-day assessment; asks about jaundice and rigors; gives a 999 safety-net; mentions ultrasound and surgery later.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: prioritises today from the first minute; surfaces the childcare barrier and solves it with her; screens for sepsis; keeps the differential open; uses teach-back and arranges a call-back so the plan actually happens.

avoid.dont: “Try some strong antacids and see how you go.”
avoid.instead: “Pain that won’t settle with a fever isn’t indigestion — you need to be seen today.”
avoid.why: Remote treatment with red flags present is unsafe.

avoid.dont: “You just need to go to A&E.”
avoid.instead: “Let’s sort out the children together, and I’ll refer you to the surgical team now.”
avoid.why: An instruction that ignores the barrier is unlikely to be followed.

avoid.instead: “Your usual attacks sound like gallstones — but today may be an inflamed gallbladder.”
avoid.why: “Just” undoes the urgency you need her to accept.

points.t: Pain that persists beyond about 6 hours, or comes with fever, rigors or systemic upset, suggests acute cholecystitis; add jaundice and it may be cholangitis. Both need same-day hospital assessment. Epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting raises gallstone pancreatitis.
Upper abdominal pain can be cardiac, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, hepatitis or renal. Fever and persistence mean the patient must be examined in person — a phone consultation cannot exclude these.

NICE NG253 (2025): consider sepsis in anyone with a possible infection who is unwell. Ask about breathlessness, confusion, mottled or ashen skin, and passing little urine; any high-risk feature → 999.

NICE CG188: LFTs and abdominal ultrasound for suspected gallstone disease; MRCP if the scan shows no duct stone but the duct is dilated and/or LFTs are abnormal, with endoscopic ultrasound if MRCP is inconclusive. Offer laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallbladder stones.
NICE CG188 and QS104: for acute cholecystitis, offer laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 week of diagnosis. Until surgery, advise avoiding the foods and drinks that trigger symptoms.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Identity check; open question; picked up that today is different before exploring the usual attacks.
Young children, partner away, no childcare cover — the reason for wanting a phone remedy.
Picked up “since this morning” and “feverish” despite the antacid request, and the reluctance to come in.
Idea (indigestion after rich food), the concern about the children and disruption, and the wish for antacids by phone.
Same-day in-person assessment (Murphy’s sign, temperature, jaundice, observations); later LFTs and abdominal ultrasound.
Biliary colic versus cholecystitis versus cholangitis versus pancreatitis; keeps cardiac and peptic causes in mind.
Duration over 6 hours, fever, rigors, jaundice, vomiting, confusion and other sepsis features asked about.
Gallstone disease with suspected acute cholecystitis today — shared in plain words.
Same-day acute surgical referral with the childcare barrier solved; no antacids instead; longer-term ultrasound, LFTs and cholecystectomy per NICE CG188.
Trigger-food advice until surgery; weight discussed later, not today.
999 features named; ring back if no cover; GP call-back to confirm she is on her way.

social.t: A parent alone with young children often delays care. Treat arranging cover as part of the management plan, and have a fallback if none is found.
Weeks of attacks framed as “indigestion” — gently correct the label so she seeks help sooner next time.

legal.t: She has capacity and may decline admission. If so, explain the specific risks, offer alternatives, give a clear safety-net and document an informed decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005 principles).
After an admission or cholecystectomy she may need a fit note for time off work.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in prescribing and managing medicines and devices (2021): prescribe remotely only when you have enough information to do so safely. Fever with persistent pain needs examination.
Document the referral and the call-back. If she cannot be reached, escalate rather than assume she has gone in.

community.t: Family, friends or neighbours for childcare today; if no safe cover can be found, tell the GP or hospital team so they can help plan — young children must not be left alone. Health visitor or school for ongoing family support.

redFlags: Pain over about 6 hours with fever or systemic upset — suspected acute cholecystitis
Fever or rigors with jaundice ± confusion — possible cholangitis, emergency
Sepsis features (breathless, confused, mottled, little urine) — 999 (NICE NG253)
psychosocial: Young children, partner away, no childcare
Fear that going in means everything falls apart
ice: Concern: the children and the disruption of being assessed

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Two messages: “Your usual attacks sound like gallstones, not indigestion. Today’s pain with a fever may mean the gallbladder is inflamed, and that needs assessing in hospital today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The gallbladder is a small bag that squeezes after a fatty meal. If a stone blocks the exit, it cramps — that’s your usual attack. If it stays blocked, the bag can become inflamed or infected, which is what I’m worried about today.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted a phone fix because of the children — that makes complete sense. Let’s sort them out together so you can be seen safely.”
management.psychosocial: Help her find cover now; agree a fallback if none; a GP call-back within the hour.
sharedPlan: Same-day referral to the acute surgical team for suspected cholecystitis
No antacids instead of assessment; don’t drive herself while in pain
Later: LFTs, ultrasound and laparoscopic cholecystectomy per NICE CG188
safetyNet: Rigors, jaundice, confusion, faintness, breathlessness or much worse pain → 999
Ring back if no childcare; GP call-back to confirm she is on her way

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The patient hides the key fact at the end of her opening and asks for antacids. Candidates fail by answering the request, or by giving the right instruction in a way she cannot follow.

items.fail: Recommending antacids or a PPI by phone for “indigestion”.
items.why: Persistent pain with fever suggests acute cholecystitis; remote treatment misses it. “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.”
items.fix: “Pain that won’t settle, with a fever, isn’t indigestion. You need to be seen today.”

items.fail: Spending five minutes on the chronic pattern before reaching today’s fever.
items.why: Poor prioritisation in a telephone triage station; the urgent issue must come first.
items.fix: “I want to hear about the usual attacks, but first — tell me about today.”

items.fail: Not asking about jaundice, rigors or sepsis features.
items.why: These separate cholecystitis from cholangitis or sepsis and decide between a same-day referral and 999.
items.fix: Ask directly, and if she can’t tell, ask her to check her eyes in a mirror.

items.fail: Ordering her to A&E without asking why she wants to avoid it.
items.why: “Does not explore the patient’s circumstances.” An unaddressed childcare barrier means she won’t go.
items.fix: “Is something making it hard to come in?” Then solve it with her and agree a fallback.

items.fail: Frightening her with “this could be sepsis” with no plan attached.
items.why: Fear without a route leads to paralysis or disengagement.
items.fix: Pair each concern with an action: “That’s why I’m ringing the surgical team now.”

items.fail: Ending the call without checking she knows what to do.
items.why: Time-critical plans fail silently without teach-back and follow-up.
items.fix: Teach-back, named 999 features, and a GP call-back within the hour.
